medical.title: New antibiotic combinations aim to achieve a lasting cure for persistent bacterial vaginosis
medical.summary: Researchers and clinicians from Monash University and Bayside Health's Melbourne Sexual Health Centre are testing new combinations of antibiotics to treat persistent bacterial vaginosis (BV), following their discovery that the condition is sexually transmissible.

medical.title: Elevated C-reactive protein linked to increased risk for incident heart failure, all-cause mortality
medical.summary: For adults with an increased cardiovascular risk, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are associated with an elevated risk of incident heart failure and all-cause mortality, according to a study recently published online in the International Journal of Cardiology.

medical.title: Supporting adolescent mothers in sub-Saharan Africa means supporting two generations at once
medical.summary: A new review of research from across sub-Saharan Africa found that inadequate access to food is linked to depression, suicide attempts, HIV vulnerabilities and poorer sexual and reproductive health outcomes among adolescent mothers.

medical.title: Real-world findings suggest GLP-1 drugs offer health benefits for young people with diabetes
medical.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, from Sept. 28–Oct. 2 examined the real-world use of GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) drugs in children and young people in Germany, Austria and Luxembourg.

medical.title: Mauritius is the first country to show it is reversing the type 2 diabetes epidemic using gold-standard testing
medical.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2 and published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology shows that the small island nation of Mauritius is the first country to demonstrate that it is reversing the type 2 diabetes epidemic using the gold-standard two-hour oral glucose tolerance test (2 hour OGTT).

medical.title: Daily pill could offer alternative to insulin injections for diabetes patients at cardiovascular risk
medical.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, and published in The Lancet shows that, for people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, a daily orforglipron pill had cardiovascular safety comparable to daily insulin glargine injections while providing greater improvements in weight and blood sugar control. However, gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events were more common with orforglipron, leading to more treatment discontinuations. The study was sponsored by Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of orforglipron.

medical.title: Nail detachment over four times more common among GLP-1 users, first controlled study finds
medical.summary: Nail detachment is more than four times as common among people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists as among comparable people with obesity or type 2 diabetes who are not taking the drugs, according to the first controlled study to examine their potential effects on nail health.

medical.title: Trevogrumab (anti-myostatin) can help preserve lean mass during and after semaglutide-induced weight loss
medical.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, and in press at The Lancet shows that trevogrumab, which inhibits a protein that negatively regulates muscle mass, can reduce lean mass loss during semaglutide treatment by 50% compared with semaglutide and placebo.

medical.title: Serum 25(OH)D may serve as a biomarker of disease activity in IBD
medical.summary: For patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D) may serve as a biomarker for disease activity, according to a study published online Sept. 10 in the Journal of Clinical Medicine.

medical.title: Combination therapy emerges as possible treatment for an aggressive form of kidney cancer
medical.summary: A genetic vulnerability in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most aggressive type of kidney cancer, may lend itself to a combination treatment strategy that causes the cancer cells to self-destruct, according to recent research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Two charged in scheme to sell counterfeit Ozempic—how you can spot fake meds
medical.summary: Federal prosecutors have charged two people in an alleged scheme to bring fake versions of the type 2 diabetes drug Ozempic from China and sell them to U.S. distributors.

medical.title: Precisely timed signals recreate key antibody factory features in human blood cells
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed a simple culture method that converts B cells isolated from human blood into cells resembling germinal center B cells, which refine antibodies after infection or vaccination.

medical.title: Study shows how music may help tackle addiction
medical.summary: New research has found evidence that music can alter how the brain processes emotions in people receiving treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and reduce their cravings.

medical.title: HIV patients with cancer must travel farther than others to access clinical trials
medical.summary: For people living with HIV, the road to a promising cancer treatment can be longer than it should be, literally.

medical.title: AI-guided light analysis could help assess skin cancer and reduce unnecessary biopsies
medical.summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States and among the most common worldwide. Nearly 1.5 million new cases were diagnosed globally in 2024, including nearly 340,000 melanomas. Nonmelanoma skin cancers—primarily basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)—are even more common, with 5.4 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S.

medical.title: Feeling sick may reflect widespread changes in brain activity, mouse study suggests
medical.summary: We are all familiar with that dreaded sensation: whole-body achiness and fatigue, waves of both bone-chilling cold and intense sweating that cause us to pull cozy blankets closer and only moments later kick them away. A loss of appetite turns us off even our favorite foods. This state may stem from any number of infections, but one thing is certain: our brain is telling us we are sick.

medical.title: Insurance barriers limit access to blood cancer drugs
medical.summary: Patients with blood cancers often face major insurance hurdles and significant out-of-pocket costs when trying to access specialty oral anticancer medications, according to a new nationwide study led by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

medical.title: Inhibitory brain cells balance memory detail and stability, study suggests
medical.summary: A team from the Plasticity of Brain Networks laboratory at the Institute for Neurosciences (IN), a joint center of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and the University Miguel Hernández of Elche (UMH), has identified a mechanism that allows the brain to adjust the balance between two seemingly competing needs during memory formation: incorporating new details while maintaining representations that are sufficiently consistent to avoid confusing one experience with another.

medical.title: Investigators identify a metabolic weak point in exhausted immune cells in head and neck cancer
medical.summary: Immune cells can reach head and neck tumors, but once there, many stop functioning. This helps explain why immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors—which have transformed treatment for some cancers—benefits only 17%–23% of patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. These are cancers that arise from cells lining the mouth, throat and voice box.

medical.title: Possible new target for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia treatment identified
medical.summary: Harvard Medical School researchers at Boston Children's Hospital and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have identified a new pathway that regulates the production of fetal hemoglobin, a form of hemoglobin that normally gets replaced soon after birth by adult hemoglobin.

medical.title: Viral infections can accelerate the progression of ALS, researchers find
medical.summary: A new study from McMaster University suggests that common viral infections—like influenza or COVID-19—may accelerate the onset and progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.

science.title: Confronting demons: How acoustic and AI technology brought ancient Etruscan tombs back to life
science.summary: Although it is not always obvious, sound guides how we experience the world around us. And the latest archaeoacoustic techniques show that even the world's earliest architects understood this.

science.title: Key protein for cells' gene regulation needs a chaperone to do its job
science.summary: A protein that's essential to every cell's ability to turn off unnecessary genes is well known for its key function of compacting genes and its connection to cancer when it undergoes mutation. But until now, scientists weren't quite sure how the protein gets where it needs to go to keep genes bound up so they aren't activated.

science.title: The real cost of coal mines to people and planet
science.summary: The longer it takes to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, the more costs accrue as climate change accelerates.

science.title: Catch a rare lunar occultation of Jupiter plus Saturn at opposition in early October
science.summary: It's a busy skywatching month ahead. The first full week of October sees two top-notch skywatching events, with Saturn reaching opposition and the moon occulting Jupiter for North America on Oct. 6.

science.title: Fluorescent sensors could help researchers see diabetes in action
science.summary: Researchers from the University of Bath have developed fluorescent molecular probes that can detect changes in glucose levels inside living animals, giving scientists new ways of visualizing sugar uptake and studying diabetes, cancer and other metabolic diseases in whole organisms in real time. The findings are published in the journal Advanced Science.

science.title: Digging deep, researchers find high-altitude glacier endured last ice age
science.summary: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study.

science.title: Border entry reveals gap in international human rights law, new analysis argues
science.summary: International human rights law protects migrants once they are within a state's jurisdiction but stops short of recognizing the right to enter another country, according to a new analysis in the International Journal of Migration and Border Studies that argues this makes the system incomplete.

science.title: AI scientist autonomously generates and validates new biological discoveries
science.summary: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results. Making new biological discoveries with minimal human intervention is an important advance in self-driving laboratories.

science.title: Short on time? It could be good for you
science.summary: When it comes to mental health, it may not be how much time you have that matters, but rather how you feel about the time you have. That's one key takeaway of a new University of Colorado Boulder study examining the relationship between time and mental health.

science.title: Tracking the fin whale and the sperm whale in the Mediterranean
science.summary: Where are the great marine animals of the Mediterranean, such as the fin whale, the sperm whale or the bottlenose dolphin? How does their distribution change over a few weeks? All indications suggest that these species shift between marine areas in a remarkably short time and over relatively small spatial scales. Some species, such as the striped dolphin, maintain a relatively stable presence in certain areas, while others, such as the fin whale, move and concentrate in different areas from one observation campaign to the next.

science.title: Anti-fibrotic drug could be repurposed to control cell communication
science.summary: An experimental antifibrotic compound can dramatically alter how cells release the microscopic packages they use to communicate, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that the compound, SD-208, which reduces scar tissue in organs, substantially reduced the release of extracellular vesicles, microscopic packages that cells use to carry proteins and other biological signals to neighboring and distant cells.

science.title: Help Overlap Zoo Reveal Cosmic Dust
science.summary: Galaxies, vast collections of billions of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, are scattered across the immensity of space. But every so often, a coincidence occurs: Two galaxies line up from our point of view on Earth (or from a space telescope) and appear to overlap in the sky. These rare overlapping galaxies […]

science.title: NASA Adds New Science Investigations for Moon Base
science.summary: NASA selected three new scientific investigations and their payload suites to advance our knowledge of the Moon and help pave the way for building humanity’s first lunar outpost, Moon Base. The suite of science instruments and technologies was selected through NASA’s Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program and will […]

science.title: Scientists in 1960 predicted Friday 13 November 2026 will be 'Doomsday.' Should you be worried?
science.summary: In 1960, Science, one of the world's leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.

science.title: 1 in 2 Florida residents live in HOAs—how these private governments are reshaping the American Dream
science.summary: As she sat across from me drinking tea, Coretta—a pseudonym to protect her identity—shared her dismay about living in a central Florida community because of the control exercised by her homeowners association, or HOA.

science.title: Fossil long known as world's oldest reptile dethroned
science.summary: For nearly 30 years, a small fossil from Scotland has been celebrated as one of the earliest known reptiles. A new study out today in Nature and led by researchers at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, is rewriting that story.

science.title: 'Molecular movie' fills in blanks of how nonenveloped viruses infect cells
science.summary: Viruses come in two major flavors—not chocolate and vanilla, quips Harvard Medical School structural biologist Stephen Harrison, but those enveloped in membranes, such as herpesvirus, influenza virus, HIV and SARS-CoV-2, and those that are not, such as poliovirus, HPV, rotavirus and adenovirus.

science.title: Classifying groundwater systems by their ability to recover from drought
science.summary: A few days of rain do not change low groundwater levels after a long drought. To better determine how groundwater systems recover after a drought and which groundwater reserves are most vulnerable, hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth developed a method to classify groundwater systems based on their ability to recover from prolonged drought.

science.title: Clay tablets reveal how Babylonian students learned about their gods
science.summary: When it came to religious education in ancient Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, students had a lot to learn, ranging from the names of gods to their divine characteristics. A new study published in the journal Iraq has taken a deep dive into ancient texts and surviving clay tablets to find out just how these traditions were taught in the classroom.

science.title: Some threatened species may miss out as zoos try to balance conservation efforts with competing pressures
science.summary: In the largest study of its kind, researchers at Nottingham Trent University analyzed more than 7,200 species across 613 zoos in 72 countries over a 30-year period. The team compared changes in zoo animal holdings with changes in species' conservation status, including extinction risk, international trade protections and involvement in zoo conservation breeding programs.

science.title: Mouse study reveals magnetic nanoparticles' potential for ectopic pregnancy diagnosis and treatment
science.summary: A research team led by an Oregon State University scientist has demonstrated in a mouse model a potentially better way to care for women facing the life-threatening condition of ectopic pregnancy.

science.title: Wood beneath German lake may reveal buildings 3,000 years older than region's first farms
science.summary: Underwater archaeological investigations have been taking place in Lake Arendsee (Altmarkkreis Salzwedel) for several years. The discovery of Neolithic fish weirs, a high medieval barge (flat-bottomed cargo ship) and a late medieval dugout canoe attracted considerable attention.

science.title: Groups of genetically identical fish follow different behavioral paths as they mature
science.summary: Schooling fish have long fascinated us with their mesmerizing collective movements and seemingly perfect coordination. But a new study on clonal mollies suggests that this behavior is not innate. During their first days of life, the fish still display distinct individual behaviors, and it is only around one month of age that they begin to form cohesive shoals, developing the coordinated movements characteristic of the group. However, several shoals of genetically identical clones begin to behave differently after a few weeks.

science.title: UV light locks radiation-detecting materials into durable, water-resistant films
science.summary: Florida State University researchers have developed a method to make a class of materials more robust and potentially easier to manufacture for advanced radiation detection devices, including those used in medical imaging and radiation therapy as well as space technologies.

science.title: Stratospheric observatory Sunrise-III reveals intricate solar magnetic structures
science.summary: A team of researchers led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan discovered unexpectedly intricate magnetic structures above quiet-sun regions by observing the sun with the balloon-borne solar observatory Sunrise-III during its 2024 flight in Earth's stratosphere. The work is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
environment.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

environment.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

environment.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
environment.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

environment.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
environment.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Confronting demons: How acoustic and AI technology brought ancient Etruscan tombs back to life
mix_items.summary: Although it is not always obvious, sound guides how we experience the world around us. And the latest archaeoacoustic techniques show that even the world's earliest architects understood this.

mix_items.title: Key protein for cells' gene regulation needs a chaperone to do its job
mix_items.summary: A protein that's essential to every cell's ability to turn off unnecessary genes is well known for its key function of compacting genes and its connection to cancer when it undergoes mutation. But until now, scientists weren't quite sure how the protein gets where it needs to go to keep genes bound up so they aren't activated.

mix_items.title: New antibiotic combinations aim to achieve a lasting cure for persistent bacterial vaginosis
mix_items.summary: Researchers and clinicians from Monash University and Bayside Health's Melbourne Sexual Health Centre are testing new combinations of antibiotics to treat persistent bacterial vaginosis (BV), following their discovery that the condition is sexually transmissible.

mix_items.title: Elevated C-reactive protein linked to increased risk for incident heart failure, all-cause mortality
mix_items.summary: For adults with an increased cardiovascular risk, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are associated with an elevated risk of incident heart failure and all-cause mortality, according to a study recently published online in the International Journal of Cardiology.

mix_items.title: The real cost of coal mines to people and planet
mix_items.summary: The longer it takes to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, the more costs accrue as climate change accelerates.

mix_items.title: Supporting adolescent mothers in sub-Saharan Africa means supporting two generations at once
mix_items.summary: A new review of research from across sub-Saharan Africa found that inadequate access to food is linked to depression, suicide attempts, HIV vulnerabilities and poorer sexual and reproductive health outcomes among adolescent mothers.

mix_items.title: Real-world findings suggest GLP-1 drugs offer health benefits for young people with diabetes
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, from Sept. 28–Oct. 2 examined the real-world use of GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) drugs in children and young people in Germany, Austria and Luxembourg.

mix_items.title: Mauritius is the first country to show it is reversing the type 2 diabetes epidemic using gold-standard testing
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2 and published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology shows that the small island nation of Mauritius is the first country to demonstrate that it is reversing the type 2 diabetes epidemic using the gold-standard two-hour oral glucose tolerance test (2 hour OGTT).

mix_items.title: Daily pill could offer alternative to insulin injections for diabetes patients at cardiovascular risk
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, and published in The Lancet shows that, for people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, a daily orforglipron pill had cardiovascular safety comparable to daily insulin glargine injections while providing greater improvements in weight and blood sugar control. However, gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events were more common with orforglipron, leading to more treatment discontinuations. The study was sponsored by Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of orforglipron.

mix_items.title: Nail detachment over four times more common among GLP-1 users, first controlled study finds
mix_items.summary: Nail detachment is more than four times as common among people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists as among comparable people with obesity or type 2 diabetes who are not taking the drugs, according to the first controlled study to examine their potential effects on nail health.

mix_items.title: Trevogrumab (anti-myostatin) can help preserve lean mass during and after semaglutide-induced weight loss
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, and in press at The Lancet shows that trevogrumab, which inhibits a protein that negatively regulates muscle mass, can reduce lean mass loss during semaglutide treatment by 50% compared with semaglutide and placebo.

mix_items.title: Catch a rare lunar occultation of Jupiter plus Saturn at opposition in early October
mix_items.summary: It's a busy skywatching month ahead. The first full week of October sees two top-notch skywatching events, with Saturn reaching opposition and the moon occulting Jupiter for North America on Oct. 6.

mix_items.title: Fluorescent sensors could help researchers see diabetes in action
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Bath have developed fluorescent molecular probes that can detect changes in glucose levels inside living animals, giving scientists new ways of visualizing sugar uptake and studying diabetes, cancer and other metabolic diseases in whole organisms in real time. The findings are published in the journal Advanced Science.

mix_items.title: Digging deep, researchers find high-altitude glacier endured last ice age
mix_items.summary: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study.

mix_items.title: Border entry reveals gap in international human rights law, new analysis argues
mix_items.summary: International human rights law protects migrants once they are within a state's jurisdiction but stops short of recognizing the right to enter another country, according to a new analysis in the International Journal of Migration and Border Studies that argues this makes the system incomplete.

mix_items.title: AI scientist autonomously generates and validates new biological discoveries
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results. Making new biological discoveries with minimal human intervention is an important advance in self-driving laboratories.

mix_items.title: Serum 25(OH)D may serve as a biomarker of disease activity in IBD
mix_items.summary: For patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D) may serve as a biomarker for disease activity, according to a study published online Sept. 10 in the Journal of Clinical Medicine.

mix_items.title: Combination therapy emerges as possible treatment for an aggressive form of kidney cancer
mix_items.summary: A genetic vulnerability in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most aggressive type of kidney cancer, may lend itself to a combination treatment strategy that causes the cancer cells to self-destruct, according to recent research published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Short on time? It could be good for you
mix_items.summary: When it comes to mental health, it may not be how much time you have that matters, but rather how you feel about the time you have. That's one key takeaway of a new University of Colorado Boulder study examining the relationship between time and mental health.

mix_items.title: Tracking the fin whale and the sperm whale in the Mediterranean
mix_items.summary: Where are the great marine animals of the Mediterranean, such as the fin whale, the sperm whale or the bottlenose dolphin? How does their distribution change over a few weeks? All indications suggest that these species shift between marine areas in a remarkably short time and over relatively small spatial scales. Some species, such as the striped dolphin, maintain a relatively stable presence in certain areas, while others, such as the fin whale, move and concentrate in different areas from one observation campaign to the next.

mix_items.title: Anti-fibrotic drug could be repurposed to control cell communication
mix_items.summary: An experimental antifibrotic compound can dramatically alter how cells release the microscopic packages they use to communicate, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that the compound, SD-208, which reduces scar tissue in organs, substantially reduced the release of extracellular vesicles, microscopic packages that cells use to carry proteins and other biological signals to neighboring and distant cells.

mix_items.title: Two charged in scheme to sell counterfeit Ozempic—how you can spot fake meds
mix_items.summary: Federal prosecutors have charged two people in an alleged scheme to bring fake versions of the type 2 diabetes drug Ozempic from China and sell them to U.S. distributors.

mix_items.title: Precisely timed signals recreate key antibody factory features in human blood cells
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed a simple culture method that converts B cells isolated from human blood into cells resembling germinal center B cells, which refine antibodies after infection or vaccination.

mix_items.title: Help Overlap Zoo Reveal Cosmic Dust
mix_items.summary: Galaxies, vast collections of billions of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, are scattered across the immensity of space. But every so often, a coincidence occurs: Two galaxies line up from our point of view on Earth (or from a space telescope) and appear to overlap in the sky. These rare overlapping galaxies […]

mix_items.title: NASA Adds New Science Investigations for Moon Base
mix_items.summary: NASA selected three new scientific investigations and their payload suites to advance our knowledge of the Moon and help pave the way for building humanity’s first lunar outpost, Moon Base. The suite of science instruments and technologies was selected through NASA’s Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program and will […]

mix_items.title: Scientists in 1960 predicted Friday 13 November 2026 will be 'Doomsday.' Should you be worried?
mix_items.summary: In 1960, Science, one of the world's leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.

mix_items.title: 1 in 2 Florida residents live in HOAs—how these private governments are reshaping the American Dream
mix_items.summary: As she sat across from me drinking tea, Coretta—a pseudonym to protect her identity—shared her dismay about living in a central Florida community because of the control exercised by her homeowners association, or HOA.

mix_items.title: Study shows how music may help tackle addiction
mix_items.summary: New research has found evidence that music can alter how the brain processes emotions in people receiving treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and reduce their cravings.

mix_items.title: HIV patients with cancer must travel farther than others to access clinical trials
mix_items.summary: For people living with HIV, the road to a promising cancer treatment can be longer than it should be, literally.

mix_items.title: Fossil long known as world's oldest reptile dethroned
mix_items.summary: For nearly 30 years, a small fossil from Scotland has been celebrated as one of the earliest known reptiles. A new study out today in Nature and led by researchers at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, is rewriting that story.

mix_items.title: 'Molecular movie' fills in blanks of how nonenveloped viruses infect cells
mix_items.summary: Viruses come in two major flavors—not chocolate and vanilla, quips Harvard Medical School structural biologist Stephen Harrison, but those enveloped in membranes, such as herpesvirus, influenza virus, HIV and SARS-CoV-2, and those that are not, such as poliovirus, HPV, rotavirus and adenovirus.

mix_items.title: Classifying groundwater systems by their ability to recover from drought
mix_items.summary: A few days of rain do not change low groundwater levels after a long drought. To better determine how groundwater systems recover after a drought and which groundwater reserves are most vulnerable, hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth developed a method to classify groundwater systems based on their ability to recover from prolonged drought.

mix_items.title: Clay tablets reveal how Babylonian students learned about their gods
mix_items.summary: When it came to religious education in ancient Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, students had a lot to learn, ranging from the names of gods to their divine characteristics. A new study published in the journal Iraq has taken a deep dive into ancient texts and surviving clay tablets to find out just how these traditions were taught in the classroom.

mix_items.title: AI-guided light analysis could help assess skin cancer and reduce unnecessary biopsies
mix_items.summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States and among the most common worldwide. Nearly 1.5 million new cases were diagnosed globally in 2024, including nearly 340,000 melanomas. Nonmelanoma skin cancers—primarily basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)—are even more common, with 5.4 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S.

mix_items.title: Some threatened species may miss out as zoos try to balance conservation efforts with competing pressures
mix_items.summary: In the largest study of its kind, researchers at Nottingham Trent University analyzed more than 7,200 species across 613 zoos in 72 countries over a 30-year period. The team compared changes in zoo animal holdings with changes in species' conservation status, including extinction risk, international trade protections and involvement in zoo conservation breeding programs.

mix_items.title: Mouse study reveals magnetic nanoparticles' potential for ectopic pregnancy diagnosis and treatment
mix_items.summary: A research team led by an Oregon State University scientist has demonstrated in a mouse model a potentially better way to care for women facing the life-threatening condition of ectopic pregnancy.

mix_items.title: Feeling sick may reflect widespread changes in brain activity, mouse study suggests
mix_items.summary: We are all familiar with that dreaded sensation: whole-body achiness and fatigue, waves of both bone-chilling cold and intense sweating that cause us to pull cozy blankets closer and only moments later kick them away. A loss of appetite turns us off even our favorite foods. This state may stem from any number of infections, but one thing is certain: our brain is telling us we are sick.

mix_items.title: Wood beneath German lake may reveal buildings 3,000 years older than region's first farms
mix_items.summary: Underwater archaeological investigations have been taking place in Lake Arendsee (Altmarkkreis Salzwedel) for several years. The discovery of Neolithic fish weirs, a high medieval barge (flat-bottomed cargo ship) and a late medieval dugout canoe attracted considerable attention.

mix_items.title: Groups of genetically identical fish follow different behavioral paths as they mature
mix_items.summary: Schooling fish have long fascinated us with their mesmerizing collective movements and seemingly perfect coordination. But a new study on clonal mollies suggests that this behavior is not innate. During their first days of life, the fish still display distinct individual behaviors, and it is only around one month of age that they begin to form cohesive shoals, developing the coordinated movements characteristic of the group. However, several shoals of genetically identical clones begin to behave differently after a few weeks.

mix_items.title: UV light locks radiation-detecting materials into durable, water-resistant films
mix_items.summary: Florida State University researchers have developed a method to make a class of materials more robust and potentially easier to manufacture for advanced radiation detection devices, including those used in medical imaging and radiation therapy as well as space technologies.

mix_items.title: Insurance barriers limit access to blood cancer drugs
mix_items.summary: Patients with blood cancers often face major insurance hurdles and significant out-of-pocket costs when trying to access specialty oral anticancer medications, according to a new nationwide study led by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

mix_items.title: Stratospheric observatory Sunrise-III reveals intricate solar magnetic structures
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan discovered unexpectedly intricate magnetic structures above quiet-sun regions by observing the sun with the balloon-borne solar observatory Sunrise-III during its 2024 flight in Earth's stratosphere. The work is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

mix_items.title: Inhibitory brain cells balance memory detail and stability, study suggests
mix_items.summary: A team from the Plasticity of Brain Networks laboratory at the Institute for Neurosciences (IN), a joint center of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and the University Miguel Hernández of Elche (UMH), has identified a mechanism that allows the brain to adjust the balance between two seemingly competing needs during memory formation: incorporating new details while maintaining representations that are sufficiently consistent to avoid confusing one experience with another.

mix_items.title: Investigators identify a metabolic weak point in exhausted immune cells in head and neck cancer
mix_items.summary: Immune cells can reach head and neck tumors, but once there, many stop functioning. This helps explain why immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors—which have transformed treatment for some cancers—benefits only 17%–23% of patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. These are cancers that arise from cells lining the mouth, throat and voice box.

mix_items.title: Possible new target for sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia treatment identified
mix_items.summary: Harvard Medical School researchers at Boston Children's Hospital and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have identified a new pathway that regulates the production of fetal hemoglobin, a form of hemoglobin that normally gets replaced soon after birth by adult hemoglobin.

mix_items.title: Viral infections can accelerate the progression of ALS, researchers find
mix_items.summary: A new study from McMaster University suggests that common viral infections—like influenza or COVID-19—may accelerate the onset and progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
